articles.title: AI agents that shop for you are changing how retail advertising works
articles.text:
AI shopping agents are shifting the retail advertising landscape
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 27, 2026
AI agents that shop for you are changing how retail advertising works
Early data from Adobe shows AI referrals to retail sites were up more than 150% over last year — but when bots do the browsing, they’re less susceptible to online ads geared to humans.
Retailby Meghan McCarty Carino
Download
Latin American woman at home buying clothes online on her cell phone and paying by credit card
Hispanolistic/Getty Images
As the holiday shopping season officially kicks off this Black Friday, it’s clear AI is becoming a bigger part of the consumer tradition. Early data from Adobe show AI referrals to retail sites yesterday were up more than 150% over last year.
It’s the first holiday season consumers have been equipped with widely available artificial intelligence personal assistants, like Meta’s Muse, that can actually do all the deal hunting and complete purchases. But adding bots into the shopping process could complicate a part of the retail business that has become increasingly lucrative: advertising.
AI personal assistants can help make us savvier shoppers this holiday season, said Koen Pauwels, a marketing professor at Northeastern University.
“I want my digital twin to look at all the possible deals out there in this Black Friday, and kind of alert me to stuff that I don't have time for,” he said.
If you give them your banking information, AI assistants can make purchases on your behalf. So you could check off your shopping list without ever browsing a single retail site yourself.
“That also makes it much more complicated for brands and retailers to somehow affect or influence our choices,” Pauwels said.
AI and shopping
From November 2026 AI agents are here to help with your online shopping (where they're allowed)
From November 2026 Why bans on surveillance pricing are gaining traction
From September 2026 "The heart of the internet": AI has marketers flocking to Reddit
From December 2025 Shoppers are increasingly using AI to find deals, recommendations
A human shopper will run into sponsored search results and banner ads. And for retailers, selling advertising has much bigger margins than selling stuff.
Some retailers, like Amazon, have blocked AI agents like Muse.
Because if only bots are seeing the ads? “They're typically more consistent and rational than we humans are,” Pauwels said.
AI isn’t susceptible to impulse spending. So ads targeting bots need to be less emotional, more transactional, said retail consultant Katherine Black at Kearney.
“It might become more like a bidding system where advertisers are sort of bidding to be included, or they're bidding to maybe even offer the lowest price to win a sale,” she said.
Most shoppers aren’t yet willing to hand over their wallets to bots, said Andrew Lipsman, an independent commerce analyst. He said instead, most consumers are using AI to discover products and track deals, then clicking ‘buy’ themselves.
“It helps consumers build conviction in their purchase. And under that scenario, every engagement on an e-commerce site becomes more valuable,” Lipsman said.
While ads might not get in front of as many human eyeballs, he said the ones they do reach are ready to buy.

articles.title: Hunting and foraging classes gain popularity, as more people want to connect with nature
articles.text:
Why hunting and foraging are gaining popularity
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 27, 2026
Hunting and foraging classes gain popularity, as more people want to connect with nature
People have harvested wild foods for millennia. These groups are teaching people to eat "field to fork" again.
Agricultureby Celia Llopis-Jepsen
Download
Above, Leonore Enfield aims a crossbow at a target. She hit the bull’s-eye with both of her first-ever shots. Enfield and her fellow Wild Foods Academy graduates committed to becoming wild foods instructors.
Celia Llopis-Jepsen/Harvest Public Media
This story was first published by Harvest Public Media.
Leonore Enfield tried for the first time last fall to shoot a deer. She spent a full day sitting in an elevated stand near Lawrence, Kansas, with an experienced hunter as mentor.
“We did not get a single thing,” Enfield said, laughing. “It was totally worth it.”
The two of them watched the sun rise and set. They drank hot chocolate and ate snacks. They sat quietly with their crossbows for long periods, eyes and ears trained on their surroundings, whispering about movements in the distance. Enfield never got bored.
“The birds started chirping,” she recalled. “You got to see just the movement of life around you — undisturbed — and so it was amazing.”
Enfield said the experience of hunting can give a meal a deeper meaning.
“It’s, like, primal,” she said. “It’s like those basic things that everybody can relate to, but very few people nowadays understand.”
Humans have fished, foraged, and hunted for millennia, but those activities have been sidelined in the modern U.S., where much of the population no longer eats any wild foods. Now, the knowledge of how to track down your own sustenance is being sought after by people who want to strengthen their connection to plants, animals, and landscapes.
Ethnobotanist Linda Black Elk has seen a surge in people seeking foraging skills. She studies and teaches about relationships between plants and humans, and works for the Minnesota-based, Native-led North American Traditional Indigenous Food Systems, or NATIFS.
“It is absolutely wild how many requests for plant walks and educational materials we get,” said Black Elk, the nonprofit’s director of education. “It is literally every day.”
People reach out in search of workshops and information about harvesting specific plants. The group publishes illustrated cards and posts detailed videos on foraging and cooking for each region of the country. Its goal is to improve access to Indigenous foods — especially for Native people — and to support tribal food sovereignty.
More on the hunting and foraging economy
From October 2026: Hunters have to hunt for a place to turn wild game into food
From November 2025: marketplace.org/story/2025/11/07/one-minnesota-business-slice-of-the-mushroom-economy
From August 2023: Debunking the myth of the male hunter
Wild plants and proteins can lower a family’s grocery bill, provide medicines, promote fairness in food systems, and offer a sense of place, Black Elk said.
“My grandmother used to say that you know you’re not home when you don’t know the plants outside your door,” Black Elk said. “So if you want to feel at home somewhere — learn those plants, build those relationships.”
Black Elk, who is not a tribal member, was raised with wild food traditions on both sides of her family. Her mother grew up in South Korea, where she foraged to put food on the table, and her father’s mother was a Southerner who loved pokeweed and wild onions.
“ One of my very first memories is harvesting wild onions with my grandmother,” she said.
Enfield graduated this summer from a pilot program that teaches Kansans to harvest, process, and eat wild foods legally, sustainably, and safely. Much like a master gardener program, those who complete the Wild Foods Academy commit to volunteering in their communities to show others how to eat “field to fork.”
“It helps people to be connected to each other, to the land,” said Enfield, who works at the Kansas Association for Conservation and Environmental Education. “When you can do that, then you’re more filled, more well-rounded, more connected.”
A short-staffed state agency gets a wild idea
When the Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks started holding workshops on easily accessible wild sources of protein, the events drew plenty of interest. Just a few generations ago, wild rabbit and squirrel were common fare, but over the decades, they’ve vanished from many dinner tables.
One training session on how to trap, kill, process and cook squirrels attracted more than 60 people in Lawrence. Just as many people came to a similar workshop at Hillsdale State Park on raccoons, where attendees gobbled up homemade “racquitos” — raccoon taquitos.
Amy Bousman, who works at the department, taught those workshops (and made those racquitos). She said small animals are some of the most accessible sources of wild protein. A squirrel trap is cheaper than hunting equipment. It also works well for people with mobility issues who may not be able to lug hunting gear through woods.
Amy Bousman, left, prepares a dead squirrel at a 2023 workshop in Lawrence on trapping, processing and cooking them. Bousman works for the Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks.
Celia Llopis-Jepsen/Harvest Public Media
She’s also seen lots of interest in learning how to gig — or spear — frogs.
This raises the question of how to make it easy for more people to learn. The wildlife department is a relatively small agency and can’t meet all the requests for events on gathering mushrooms and wild greens, for example.
“There’s just not staff capacity,” Bousman said. “There’s no shortage of interest, but there is a shortage of qualified and available people to lead those kinds of classes.”

articles.title: Why in the world do airlines overbook tickets?
articles.text:
Why in the world do airlines overbook tickets?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 27, 2026Updated Nov 27, 2026, 5:52 pm
Why in the world do airlines overbook tickets?
It's intentional, and not totally evil — it might even be good.
I've Always Wondered ...by Sabri Ben-Achour
A new study looks at the cost of add-on charges for airlines.
Joe Raedle/Getty Images
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here.
This article originally ran on April 27, 2015.
Lamonte Freerks asks:
I would like to know why airlines see the need to overbook planes, thus at times bumping paid passengers.”
Destination: Irony. Temperature at destination: Cruel
The irony was not lost on Danielle Sharp as the announcement came on over the loudspeaker at 5:30 a.m. at Newark airport.
“United, Flight 3454, is now boarding.”
Danielle Sharp was most definitely not boarding. Though paid and checked in for a trip to Oklahoma, her ticket had also been sold to someone else.
“The flight is overbooked, so we’re just sitting here waiting. The flight is leaving in 15 minutes and we’re just stuck here,” she says when reached at the airport. “It’s really stressful and aggravating. I got here at 3 a.m. for a 6 o’clock flight.”
Why would an airline do this? How hard is it to count the number of seats on a plane and not sell more than that?
“I have no idea,” Sharp says, resigned. “But it’s obvious they care more about their money than they care about us, ’cause they wouldn’t inconvenience us like this. It’s about a buck.”
Yes … and no.
Why do they do it?
“Contrary to what popular perception may be, airlines are not evil,” says Samuel Engel, who leads the Aviation Practice at consulting firm ICF international. It’s not an accident that airlines overbook their flights, and it boils down to one simple reason: “Some passengers don’t show up.”
In fact, some passengers are almost always not going to show up.
“So if you know that’s going to be the case, you’re setting yourself up for flying with empty seats and wasting them,” says Engel.
But wait, if people don’t show up, aren’t the airlines then just selling the same seat twice and making gobs of money off of the poor jerks who are left behind when people actually do all show up?
No, says Engel, because the airlines “don’t get revenue for a seat that goes empty.” It’s true someone has paid for that seat, but in most cases that person will end up being given a free flight by the airline to accommodate them if they were just running late, for example.
“Some passengers will just not show up because they didn’t want to take the trip, but more cases than not, they arrived at the airport 15 minutes late ’cause there was traffic and they missed their flight and the airline is going to accommodate them on another flight.”
The guessing game
So if airlines didn’t overbook, they would lose money, so they actually put a lot of effort and money into guessing exactly how many people won’t show up on a given flight.
“Virtually all airlines these days have fairly sophisticated revenue management systems,” says Peter Belobaba, a research scientist at the International Center for Air Transportation at MIT. Revenue management system means really complicated computer models.
These models predict a lot of things: how many seats should the airline sell for cheaper to people who buy earlier? How many can it get away with setting aside in order to charge higher prices for last-minute business travelers? How many people won’t show up? In the event everyone with a ticket does show up, how many people will accept a voucher for free miles in order to take a different flight?
For the no-show predictions, “those systems have large historical databases of no-show rates on previous departures of the same time of day and in the same markets, used to build forecasts,” says Belobaba.
With the advent of big data, airlines can feed even more information into their models.
“People returning from a long weekend are more likely to show up as compared to people who are starting their trip for business. How long ago you bought your ticket, has it been ticketed, those all can be correlated with no show behavior,” says Belobaba.
The cutting edge models, says ICF International’s Samuel Engel, also take into account the competing fares at any given moment from competitor airlines. If every airline is eyeing what one another is doing, things can get quite complicated.
“It’s a field of very happy geeks mired in the data balancing the statistics and economics trying to make better decisions,” says Engel.
RELATED:
United CEO Oscar Munoz on making flying less horrible
A little over a year ago, United was looking for a comeback
What have you always wondered? Tell us and check out our series, I’ve Always Wondered
Subscribe to the Marketplace podcast with Kai Ryssdal
They are actually pretty good at guessing
It turns out, those models work pretty well.
“If you look back, you’ll see the U.S. airline industry has reduced the denied boarding rate almost in half in the last 15 years,” says Engel. “In 1999, 0.2 percent of passengers were denied boarding. In 2014, it was under 0.1 percent. And only 1/10th of those were ‘involuntarily denied boarding,’ where passengers did not choose to take a different flight” in exchange for a voucher or incentive.
United Airlines, whose flight Danielle Sharp was bumped off of, says much of the 1/10th of 1/10th of one percent of involuntary denied boarding is due to grounded planes and not overbooking. The outliers usually occur when there is an unexpected disruption, like weather, a problem at an airport, or some other factor.
Maybe it’s a good thing

articles.title: White House announces new tariffs on China, EU, and more
articles.text:
Trump's latest tariff push: What are the details?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 25, 2026
White House announces new tariffs on China, EU, and more
The proposed duties range from 15% to 35% and could cover roughly three-fifths of U.S. imports.
Trade War 2.0by Associated Press
The tariffs will largely replace those first imposed last April and should have a modest impact on inflation and growth, economists said.
Peter W. Stevenson/The Washington Post via Getty Images
The Trump administration announced a set of broad new tariffs Wednesday on imports from China, the European Union, Taiwan and 11 other countries in response to their alleged overproduction of factory goods that have disadvantaged American firms.
The new tariffs are also intended to help replace the revenue lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that President Donald Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, told CNBC that many U.S. trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The proposed duties range from 15% to 35% and could cover roughly three-fifths of U.S. imports, though the administration also proposed exemptions for products such as semiconductors and other high-tech goods from Taiwan and South Korea, which are crucial to the artificial intelligence buildout.
While sweeping, the tariffs largely replace those first imposed last April and should have a modest impact on inflation and growth, economists said.
The duties “were widely expected, are relatively small, and would return us roughly to where we were earlier in the year,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, said.
Yet the announcement demonstrates the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.
“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
The administration will next seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing January 25, suggesting the duties won’t take effect until February or March.
Tariffs may be here to stay despite electoral sweep
Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the Finance Committee next year, said he will “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
Still, any effort to overturn them faces steep odds, even after Democrats take control of both chambers in January. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
The small business advocacy group We Pay the Tariffs, which urged Congress to roll back all tariffs after the election, slammed Wednesday’s maneuver.
“Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses,” Dan Anthony, executive director of the group, said in a prepared statement. “Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top of tariffs either.”
Brazil and China will face some of the biggest hits
The levies will be imposed pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.
The administration said the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.
Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after trade talks stalled. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
Brazil’s government expressed indignation over the proposed tariffs and threatened retaliatory measures.
“The USTR’s unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process,” it said in a statement. “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat.”
It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
The U.S. and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could come up again.

articles.title: How to outsmart tariffs at the grocery store this holiday season
articles.text:
Budget-friendly holiday recipes advise tariff-proof swaps
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 25, 2026
How to outsmart tariffs at the grocery store this holiday season
At Budget Bytes, senior test kitchen editor Jess Rice focuses on tariff-proofing holiday recipes.
Economyby Alice Wilder
Download
Jess Rice with her holiday haul in the Budget Bytes test kitchen
Alice Wilder/Marketplace
Jess Rice starts most work days at a Walmart near her home in rural Tennessee. She’s the senior test kitchen editor at Budget Bytes, a food blog focused on affordable recipes. There, she shops for ingredients and develops delicious but frugal meals.
On Budget Bytes you’ll find over 10 years worth of recipes. None cost over $3.50 per serving to prepare. The price of groceries has increased by 30% since the pandemic, and experts say there’s no decrease in sight. But the Budget Bytes policy on affordable recipes remains the same.
“Our feet are to the fire a little bit,” Rice said. The Budget Bytes comments section is filled with readers reporting rising prices in their local grocery stores.
“ Instead of coming at this issue with gloom and doom, I wanted to give people a roadmap so they were able to feed themselves and their family well despite what was coming down the line,” Rice said.
So she and the team at Budget Bytes developed the Almost Tariff Proof Grocery Guide, which walks readers through the impact of tariffs and advises swaps that can keep costs down.
Ahead of the holiday season, Rice published an updated guide which includes a holiday meal plan that feeds eight people for under $45.
“People are gonna be full, and they are going to be so happy to spend time together and have a home cooked meal,” she said.
Rice and the team at Budget Bytes meticulously track grocery prices from their test kitchen in East Nashville, where shelves of cookware and kitchen essentials line the walls. “We just have to constantly be consuming that content.”
Though the news is rarely good, the team focuses on what they can control. “ We do believe that there's a workaround for everything, and so we try to provide solutions for people instead of making them feel like they're doing without,” Rice said.

articles.title: Why consumers are being more patient and putting off purchases
articles.text:
Why this holiday season, consumers are delaying purchases
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 25, 2026
Why consumers are being more patient and putting off purchases
Consumer spending rose 0.3% in October — and so did inflation. That basically means spending was flat, despite the run-up to the holiday season.
Retailby Kristin Schwab
Download
Consumers might be waiting to start their holiday shopping this year in search of more deals.
Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images
Consumer spending rose 0.3% in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ data from Wednesday. Inflation also rose 0.3%. In other words, spending was flat — which isn’t typical so close to the holiday shopping season.
Patience comes in many forms. And this year, consumers seem to have a lot of it.
“We see this kind of paradox with the consumer of being not confident in the future but still finding a way to keep up with spending,” said Bryan Eshelman, managing director of retail at Alix Partners.
Where there’s a will, there’s a way — and the way looks different depending on income. For higher earners, patience means holding off on the urge to splurge on a luxury bag or watch, Eshelman said.
“That is a bellwether for whether the higher income consumer is going to continue spending at the levels that they have been,” he said.
It’s a little less Canada Goose and a little more Costco. Data from Adobe Analytics shows that people spent November stocking up on essentials. Online sales of personal hygiene products alone rose by 40% compared to last year.
“It’s what’s needed,” said Jessica Ramirez, co-founder of the consulting firm The Consumer Collective. “That’s how the consumer’s shopping. It’s like, ‘I need toilet paper. I need these groceries.’”
For middle- and lower-income consumers, Ramirez said that patience is about playing the waiting game. Her research shows more than a third of these households won’t start holiday shopping until after Thanksgiving. That’s up more than 10% from last year.
“I think they’re being much more selective because they have to be,” she said. “I think that at the same time, they are hoping that there will be more discounts.”
That’s because while the holiday sales started early, consumers “also know that there’s deals all the time,” said David Swartz, a consumer equity analyst at Morningstar.
Swartz said that across income groups, patience — especially during a time when people are tempted to overspend — shows that consumers are reassessing their budgets in the long term.
“They’re probably a little bit worried that the situation is going to continue into next year and possibly beyond,” he said.
“The situation” being rising inflation — and wages that aren’t keeping up.
'Tis the season to worry about consumer spending

Marketplace Holiday Special
From budget holiday shopping and youth-run urban farms to tribal salmon fishing, wild game hunting and a family teriyaki chicken recipe with no measurements, join us for an hour of stories on the business and economics of food.
Download

The holiday meal is where family tradition meets the household budget. In this hour-long special, host Kristen Schwab digs into the food on our tables and the economy behind it. We'll shop a Tennessee Walmart with a budget-recipe developer who's working out how to feed a family of eight a holiday dinner for under $45, even with tariffs and a shrinking cattle herd jacking prices up. We'll listen in on the King Arthur Bakers Hotline as calls about ingredient substitutes and recipe mishaps pour in. And we'll visit a youth-run urban farm on Chicago's South Side, where young adults are learning job skills in a city where finding work is hard for people their age.
We'll also head into the woods of southern Maryland for a first squirrel hunt and stop by a new wild game processor in Wyoming. In Oregon, we'll meet a Native fishing family keeping tribal salmon traditions alive at their fish market on the Columbia River. In Houston, we'll see how Afghan refugees are building a thriving restaurant scene. Also, Kristen goes home to Minnesota to learn her Korean mom's famous teriyaki chicken, a dish made with no recipe, plenty of garlic and a lot of love. Together, these stories show how the holiday meal reflects what's going on in the wider economy and in our own households.
